title: Peh

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayin, the eye, and Hagar by the spring. Your line was ayin is an eye. Did the person you looked at notice? Today, the letter right after the eye: the mouth. Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

Moses is standing at the burning bush, and he has one more objection. This one is about his mouth. He tells God he has never been a man of words, that he is slow of speech and slow of tongue. A toast, a phone call, a hard conversation: the excuse has a familiar shape. God's answer is a question: who made a person's mouth? Then a promise: I will be with your mouth, and teach you what to say. The man whose words will fill so much of the Torah starts out afraid to open his. Today's letter is his mouth.

segments.voice: Peh. The word peh means a mouth, and the letter makes a p or an f sound, the sounds your lips make. Let's open it four times. First, the shape. Look at a printed peh and you may see a mouth, curved open, with a small mark tucked inside it. Some teachers say it's a tongue, waiting. Others say it's a reminder that a mouth holds something back as well as letting it out. Second, Moses. He thinks his mouth disqualifies him. God doesn't argue that he speaks well. God says the mouth was made, and that help will come into it. Third, prayer. The Amidah, the standing prayer, is opened with a short line from the Psalms. In the King James words: "O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise." The Talmud discusses saying that line there. Before the Amidah's own words begin, a person asks for help just to open their mouth. Fourth, the guard. Another psalm asks God to set a watch before the mouth and keep the door of the lips. Jewish ethics has a whole body of law about speech, lashon hara, the evil tongue, which warns against harmful talk about others even when it's true. So the mouth in this tradition is a door. It opens for praise, for teaching, for comfort. It also has a doorkeeper. The same peh that can bless can wound, and the tradition takes both seriously. Moses's slow mouth ended up carrying words people still read aloud. Yours only has to carry one kind thing today.
screen: `PEH: A MOUTH, WITH SOMETHING INSIDE.` · `MOSES: SLOW OF SPEECH.` · `OPEN MY LIPS BEFORE THE AMIDAH.` · `A DOOR, AND A DOORKEEPER.` · then, large: `O LORD, OPEN THOU MY LIPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one kind thing. Settle, and breathe. Close your mouth gently and breathe through your nose for a few breaths. Notice how much your mouth does in a day, and how rarely it rests. Now bring to mind one person who would be glad to hear something kind from you. Find the words. Keep them true, small and specific: not you're great, but the way you handled that meeting was brave. Hold the sentence ready. If you pray, you can ask for help opening your lips. The bell holds the time.
Peh. A mouth: the letter of the lips, of Moses's slow speech, and of the line said before the Amidah. Today's word.
Your line: peh is a mouth. Today, say the kind sentence you found, out loud, to the person it's for. Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Jews open the Amidah, the central standing prayer, with the verse from Psalm 51 asking God to open their lips; Jewish law on speech, lashon hara, guards against harmful talk about others.

options: that Moses is actually a fine speaker.
who made a person's mouth? I will be with your mouth.
that Moses doesn't need to speak at all.

original.note: Hebrew: mouth. The name of the letter, which makes the sound of the lips.

trapdoor: what you thought: peh is just the letter p.
what it means: peh is a mouth: Moses's slow one, the one opened before prayer, the one guarded from harm.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 4:10–12, Psalm 51:17 (51:15 in English Bibles) said before the Amidah, discussed in Berakhot 4b.

notes: Psalm 51:15 quoted from KJV; verse numbering differs in Hebrew (51:17). Confirm.
Exodus 4:10–12 paraphrased (slow of speech and slow of tongue; who made a person's mouth; I will be with your mouth). Confirm.
The shape of peh (a mark inside, read as a tongue or as restraint) is homiletic and attributed to 'some teachers'. Confirm.
Berakhot 4b discusses saying 'O Lord, open my lips' before the Amidah; cited generally. Confirm citation (also 9b).
'Moses's slow mouth ended up carrying words people still read aloud' is a general statement about the Torah reading; confirm tone.
